name: Gopal Saini
story: Gopal Saini has spent over 25 years mastering Jaipur's iconic Blue Pottery, a craft that uses no clay at all — only quartz, glass, and natural dyes. He is a National Award recipient for his work, and one of a shrinking number of artisans keeping this centuries-old Persian-influenced technique alive.
badgeReason: Fewer than 200 artisans in Jaipur still practice authentic Blue Pottery

reviews.name: Ritika Sharma
reviews.text: The vase I bought is stunning — and knowing it came straight from Gopal ji made it even more special.

reviews.name: Aman Verma
reviews.text: Took a video session to learn basic glazing — patient teacher, incredible detail.

hotspots.title: The material
hotspots.text: Made from quartz powder and glass — no clay is used at all in true Blue Pottery.

hotspots.title: The pattern
hotspots.text: The lotus motif is hand-painted using cobalt oxide, giving the signature deep blue color.

hotspots.title: The firing
hotspots.text: Fired at low temperature in a traditional kiln — too much heat and the piece cracks instantly.

hotspots.title: The technique
hotspots.text: Each plate is hand-molded, not wheel-thrown, using a mould-pressing method unique to this craft.

hotspots.title: The colors
hotspots.text: Only blue, green, and white were traditionally used — colors that stay vivid for decades.

name: Ambika Devi
story: Ambika Devi learned Madhubani painting from her mother, continuing a tradition passed down through generations of women in her village. A recipient of the National Handicrafts Award, her work often depicts nature, deities, and scenes of rural life using natural pigments made from turmeric, charcoal, and flowers.
badgeReason: Traditional natural-dye Madhubani art is increasingly replaced by synthetic paints; few artisans still use the original method

reviews.name: Nikhil Rao
reviews.text: The colors are incredible — you can tell it's natural pigment, not printed.

reviews.name: Sneha Iyer
reviews.text: Commissioned a custom piece for my mother's birthday — Ambika ji added a personal touch we didn't even ask for.

hotspots.title: The pigment
hotspots.text: Made from natural dyes — turmeric, charcoal, and flower extracts, not synthetic paint.

hotspots.title: The pattern
hotspots.text: The peacock motif symbolizes love and fertility in traditional Mithila culture.

hotspots.title: The technique
hotspots.text: Painted with a bamboo twig, not a brush — a method passed down through generations.

hotspots.title: The symbolism
hotspots.text: The Tree of Life motif represents the connection between earth, humans, and the divine.

hotspots.title: The border
hotspots.text: The double-line border filled with fish and floral patterns is a signature Madhubani style.

name: Sita Devi
story: Sita Devi is a State Award recipient known for handcrafted lac bangles, a craft involving heating natural lac resin and shaping it by hand while molten, then decorating it with mirrors, beads, and hand-painted motifs. Each piece takes hours of precise, heat-sensitive work.
badgeReason: Machine-made plastic bangles have sharply reduced demand for hand-shaped lac bangles

reviews.name: Priya Nair
reviews.text: So much detail in each bangle — you can feel the handwork.

reviews.name: Divya Menon
reviews.text: Bought a set for my wedding — completely unique, nothing like store-bought ones.

hotspots.title: The material
hotspots.text: Made from natural lac resin, heated and hand-shaped while still warm.

hotspots.title: The decoration
hotspots.text: Tiny mirrors and beads are pressed in by hand while the lac is still soft.

hotspots.title: The color
hotspots.text: Natural dyes give the deep red tone traditionally worn during festivals and weddings.

hotspots.title: The shaping
hotspots.text: Each bangle is shaped by hand on a small metal rod — no molds are used.
